title: perimeter of regular and irregular shapes

lesson.title: Walking All the Way Around: Perimeter

steps.say: Imagine your family wants to build a little fence around the vegetable garden in the backyard, so the neighbourhood rabbits stop nibbling the lettuce. Before you go to the store, you need to know one thing: how many metres of fence should we buy? That question is exactly what perimeter answers. Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape.

visual.caption: A garden bed, five metres long and three metres wide

steps.say: Here is the easiest way to think about it. Pretend you are a tiny ant walking around the edge of the garden. You walk five metres along the long side, then three metres along the short side, then five metres back, then three metres more, and you are home again. Add up every step you took: five plus three plus five plus three equals sixteen. So we need sixteen metres of fence.

Now here is a lovely shortcut. Some shapes are regular, which means all their sides are exactly the same length. Think of a square sandbox at the park, four metres on every single side. Instead of adding four plus four plus four plus four, you can just say four times four, which is sixteen. Same answer, less work!

visual.caption: A square sandbox: every side is 4 m, so perimeter = 4 x 4 = 16 m

steps.say: Shapes with three sides work the same way. Look at this triangle sign. Its bottom side is eight centimetres, and the two slanted sides are five centimetres each. Careful now, the dashed line inside is the height, and we do not walk on that. We only walk on the outside edges: eight plus five plus five equals eighteen centimetres.

visual.caption: Sides 8 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm. The dashed height is not part of the perimeter.

steps.say: In class you might use a geoboard or grid paper. Each little square is one centimetre wide, so you can just count the steps around the edge instead of measuring. On this shape, count along the bottom: one, two, three, four. Up the side: one, two, three. Then four back across the top and three back down. Four plus three plus four plus three equals fourteen centimetres.

visual.caption: On a geoboard, count the unit steps around the outside: 14 cm

steps.say: Some shapes are irregular, which just means the sides are all different lengths. There is no shortcut for those, but there is no problem either. A flower bed at the community garden has five sides that measure three metres, five metres, two metres, four metres, and six metres. We simply add them all up: three plus five is eight, plus two is ten, plus four is fourteen, plus six is twenty. Twenty metres of edging.

visual.caption: Five different sides, all added together: 20 m

steps.say: So whether a shape is regular with matching sides, or irregular and a bit wobbly, the rule never changes. Find every side, make sure you count each one exactly once, and add them all up. That total is your perimeter, and now you know exactly how much fence to buy.

visual.caption: Perimeter = add every side, once around

lesson.answer: Perimeter is the walk all the way around a shape: add up every side, exactly once.

practice.question: The Nguyen family is fencing a rectangular dog run in their Kelowna backyard. It is six metres long and four metres wide. How many metres of fencing do they need?
